segments.text: Episode sixteen. Next stop... a supernova.
A supernova is a star exploding. For a few weeks, it can outshine its entire galaxy.
segments.headline: Brighter than a galaxy

segments.text: The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that lived and died long ago.
segments.headline: You are made of stars

segments.text: In ten fifty-four, astronomers in China saw a new star so bright it was visible in daylight for weeks. Today, its remains are the Crab Nebula.
In a galaxy like ours, astronomers expect about one or two supernovae every century.
If one exploded within about fifty light-years, it could damage Earth's ozone layer. Luckily, no candidates are that close.
segments.headline: Too close for comfort?

segments.text: Tomorrow, we travel to the heart of our galaxy. Next stop: a monster black hole called Sagittarius A star. Follow, so you don't miss episode seventeen.
